name: Hidden Oasis, Wadi Shah (Jebel Jais)
area: Wadi Shah, from Jebel Jais Base Camp on the lower Jebel Jais road, Ras Al Khaimah. Also called Sal Shehhah and Wadi Khammed in some sources
gradeBasis: Visit Jebel Jais (the operator, RAK Leisure) grades its guided Hidden Oasis Walk 'beginner to intermediate', with moderate fitness needed (7km, 3.5 to 4 hours, visitjebeljais.com/jais-hiking, last checked October 2026). Its Hidden Oasis Loop (9.6km) and Hidden Pond (9km) are for experienced hikers, and its 11.6km Wadi Shah loop, which passes the Hidden Oasis at the midpoint, is 'Challenging'. For the public trail itself the operator publishes no grade. Independent grades for the walk to the oasis: Moderate in Nukta's header but 'intermediate to advanced' in its text; Moderate plus from Wikiloc commenters; Intermediate+, 7 out of 10 (ECC Adventures); 'easy to moderate' for the approach from the top of the mountain (Pinay Hakawati). Gulf News (29 October 2025) lists a longer Wadi Shah to oasis to Jais route among expert trails. Moderate is the middle of these, for the walk to the oasis and back only. Most of the effort is a long, steep climb with stairs, loose rock and sun exposure. The longer routes that continue to Shahha village, the summit or the seven-village loop are harder and are not graded here.

distanceNote: Visit Jebel Jais gives 7.0km for its guided Hidden Oasis Walk from the camp; it does not say whether that is a loop or a return trip, and it gives no distance for the public Hidden Oasis trail. Other sources: the operator's February to April 2026 listing 8.5km; Nukta 5km for a short version (and a 15km loop); Pinay Hakawati 9 to 10km return from the top of the mountain; ECC Adventures 8.7km listed as one way; Gulf News 6.9km for Wadi Shah to oasis to Jais. These are different routes and versions, so 7.0km is the operator's figure for one version only. See _doubts.
climbNote: Not confirmed. The operator gives no climb for the Hidden Oasis Walk. ECC Adventures gives 900m for its 8.7km trek and a Wikiloc author 'more than 900m', but both appear to include the climb on towards Shahha village and the Jebel Jais road. Gulf News gives 942m for the longer route to Jebel Jais and Pinay Hakawati about 689m for the approach from the top. Treat roughly 690m to 940m as the range for different versions, not as the figure for the walk to the oasis.
time: 3.5 to 4 hours (operator, guided Hidden Oasis Walk); other sources give 2 to 5 hours depending on version

trailhead.name: Wadi Shah trailhead, next to the Bear Grylls Explorers Camp (old Via Ferrata area), Jebel Jais road
trailhead.coordSource: Four independent walker sources agree within about 100m: hikerpatrick.com (25.900073, 56.141830, published 16 April 2025), two Wikiloc tracks as mirrored on loc.wiki (25.899797, 56.141828 and 25.900125, 56.141759) and Nukta's parking pin for the Hidden Oasis hike (25.8993105, 56.1420245, published 5 July 2024). None is an operator coordinate; the operator names only 'near Jebel Jais Base Camp'. The Road Reel gives a start for the Wadi Shah loop about 200m to the west (25.899871, 56.139836). No coordinate was found for the approach from the top of the mountain.
trailhead.parking: Walkers report parking next to the Bear Grylls camp or the old Via Ferrata, and one Wikiloc author says sedans can reach it. The operator does not describe a trail car park or any charge. A Wikiloc author (undated) says the road beyond a point called P-08 is for dam construction traffic only. For the top-of-mountain start, Pinay Hakawati says parking fills quickly at weekends and public holidays. Last checked October 2026.
trailhead.vehicle: 2WD to the camp area (the operator's FAQ says the Jebel Jais road is paved and a normal car is enough; a Wikiloc author says sedans park at the trailhead).

routeDescription: Naming: the names Sal Shehhah and Wadi Khammed are both used for this place in some sources, but linking them to the Hidden Oasis is probable, not confirmed. Visit Jebel Jais, Visit Ras Al Khaimah and the walkers' sources opened do not use the name Wadi Khammed. It appears in September 2026 press about the Jebel Jais trail plans (The National, Khaleej Times and Gulf News on 15 September; Emirates 24|7 on 19 September; WhatsOn on 23 September; IndexBox on 27 September), which call it another name for the Hidden Oasis at the bottom of Jebel Jais and give no map or start point. Walkers and tour operators call the oasis Sal Shuha or Sal Shahha (ECC Adventures, Alpine Trekkers, Wikiloc); no source uses the exact spelling Sal Shehhah.

This guide covers the walk up Wadi Shah to the Hidden Oasis, not the whole Wadi Shah loop. The operator's 11.6km Wadi Shah loop passes the Hidden Oasis at its midpoint and has its own guide. The operator's guided Hidden Oasis Walk from the camp is 7km and 3.5 to 4 hours. It starts and finishes at Bear Grylls Explorers Camp; the operator does not say whether it is a loop or an out-and-back.

The walk starts at the Wadi Shah trailhead beside the camp, about 450m above sea level, and heads up the wadi. The oasis point on Komoot (25.9242, 56.1547) is about 3km north-east of the trailhead pin in a straight line; that distance is my calculation. Older accounts (hikerpatrick.com, hike done in 2021) describe boulder-hopping with no path. Later accounts say dam works in the wadi removed the boulders and that a built trail, partly laid for the Highlander event and by RAKTDA, now leads to the oasis. A Wikiloc author (2024) describes stairs, zigzag paths and a trail board just past the dam. ECC Adventures describes a steady ascent with many stone staircases and cliff-side shelf paths. The operator says the first section is a steep climb.

The Hidden Oasis is a green patch of palms and fields with farming terraces. ECC Adventures and Nukta say it is greenest in winter and after rain. The Wikiloc seven-villages track lists 'Sal Shuha (Hidden Oasis)' as the first of seven villages and calls it a ruin. Walkers can extend the outing up steep stairs to Shahha village and on to the upper Jebel Jais road, but that is a longer, harder day.

A second approach starts near the last viewing deck at the top of the mountain (Pinay Hakawati, published 2022, modified March 2026). It goes downhill past an old village and down a long flight of stone steps to the oasis, then returns the same way, so the climb comes at the end. The operator does not say whether it counts this as the same trail.

Waymarking is changing. The operator says trail works and new signposts at junctions where people often get lost begin at the Hidden Oasis from October 2026, with wider paths, easier grades and better rock crossings, and the first confirmed sign locations due in mid-October. The National and Khaleej Times report the same works. Older accounts describe cairns and thin paths, and a Wikiloc reviewer reports that much of the loop from Wadi Shah is off-trail. No source says which way a loop would run or gives a turn-around point. Plan to finish well before dusk.
bestMonths: October to April (Visit Jebel Jais gives October to April as the hiking season). The oasis is greenest in winter and after rain (ECC Adventures, Nukta).
startAdvice: The operator says to start early, especially in warmer months, to avoid midday hikes and to check the weather before you set out (visitjebeljais.com/jais-hiking, last checked October 2026). The operator's own guided walks start at 08:00. ECC Adventures starts its group at 7am (about 7:15am on some dates, 6am on others). Do not plan to be on the steep sections in the heat of the day, and finish well before dark.
shade: Little. Pinay Hakawati says the upper slope and old-village section is in full sun, with trees at the oasis for resting. The operator publishes nothing on shade.
water: No reliable water source for walkers. The operator says to carry at least 3 litres per person plus rehydration drinks (visitjebeljais.com/jais-hiking, last checked October 2026). ECC Adventures says 1 to 2 litres from December to March and 2 to 3 litres the rest of the year for its guided trek; a Wikiloc author says at least 4 litres. The higher figures are safer. Pools or flowing water may appear after rain, but do not rely on them.
signal: Not confirmed. ECC Adventures says phone coverage is better than before; an Airial listing says signal can be spotty in the Jebel Jais mountains. Do not rely on it; download an offline map first.
fees: The operator says the Hidden Oasis trails are free to walk on your own (visitjebeljais.com/jais-hiking, last checked October 2026). No trail entry fee and no parking charge was found. Guided walks from the camp: Hidden Oasis Walk from AED 200 and Hidden Oasis Loop from AED 250 per adult, lower for children (operator). ECC Adventures lists its Hidden Oasis trek at AED 200 to 250 per adult and AED 150 to 200 per child for dates from 1 November 2026 to 2 January 2027, with Dubai transport extra (eccadventures.com, last checked October 2026).
permits: The operator says you do not need a guide for the Hidden Oasis trails (last checked October 2026). No individual permit was found. Groups of more than 10 must inform RAKTDA (Ras Al Khaimah Tourism Development Authority) in advance: the operator says to limit groups to 10 unless registered, and Visit Ras Al Khaimah says groups above 10 must email the authority with route, participants and timing. A Visit Ras Al Khaimah blog (December 2022, about the Wadi of the Giants hike) says RAKTDA permits only fully licensed tour operators to run such hikes.
hours: No trail opening hours found. The operator's FAQ says the mountain is open around the clock, with fixed hours only for activities such as the zipline and restaurants (last checked October 2026). That conflicts with the seasonal pause described under closure.
closure: Current status cannot be confirmed. The operator's hiking page (read 6 and 8 October 2026) says the trails are open to the public and need no guide, that trail works and signage renewal begin from October 'first at the Hidden Oasis', and that some sections may be busy while work goes in. The operator's home page still carries pause posts from summer (29 June and earlier) saying the mountain will reopen once the weather cools, with no date. WOW-RAK (a local guide site, updated 14 September 2026) says the whole mountain, including the hiking trails, is closed for seasonal maintenance with no reopening date, and quotes Marjan Lifestyle on 14 September confirming rehabilitation at Wadi Khammed and the Hidden Oasis. The National, Gulf News and Khaleej Times (15 September 2026) report rehabilitation under way at 'Wadi Khammed - Hidden Oasis', with upgrades to existing sections, new connecting trails, wider paths, easier grades, reinforced rock crossings and direction signs, continuing through the 2026/27 season with no completion date; Khaleej Times lists 'temporary signage ahead of season opening'. None of them mentions a closure of the trail itself. The works are on the route to the oasis, unlike on the full Wadi Shah loop. Storm of December 2025: The National and Gulf News (23 December 2025) said Jebel Jais operations, including the Via Ferrata and Bear Grylls Explorers Camp, were closed until further notice, while hiking and climbing areas were not formally closed and hikers were urged to avoid affected routes. Last checked October 2026. Confirm with Visit Jebel Jais (info@rakleisure.com) or the camp (+971 56 501 5831, Info@beargryllscamp.ae) before each visit.
safety: Confirm the mountain and the trail are open before you drive up. Sources read in October 2026 disagree and no reopening date is published.
Trail works are under way at the Hidden Oasis this season (operator, The National, Gulf News, Khaleej Times). Expect closed or changed sections, workers, and signs that differ from old maps.

This is a wadi route. Water flows and trail sections wash out after rain (Wikiloc author, 2024), and wadis can flood when no rain is visible nearby; Ras Al Khaimah Police warned people to stay out of valleys (Gulf News, 18 December 2025). After the December 2025 storms authorities reported standing water, shifting rocks and slippery paths and advised against camping in wadis (The National, 23 December 2025). Wadi Shah recorded 247.4mm of rain in six days in April 2019, the highest in the country in that spell (Gulf News, 16 April 2019). No source gives a flood threshold for the oasis. Do not start in or after rain.

Rescues in the Wadi Shah area are on record. Police rescued seven hikers who lost their way in Wadi Shehah on 22 February 2024, one of whom collapsed from exhaustion (Gulf Today, Dubai Eye); police airlifted an Emirati man stranded at about 2,000 feet in Wadi Shah on 15 July 2026 (Gulf News, Khaleej Times, Al Khaleej); and nine people were rescued in the Shah area on 8 April 2021 (Emarat Al Youm). None of these reports names the Hidden Oasis, so the exact spots are not known. After the 2024 rescue police advised telling the authorities where you are going before a recreational trip.

Heat: the operator advises October to April and says to avoid midday hiking in warmer months. Do not walk this route in summer. A British hiker died after a fall on Jebel Jais on a 45 degree day in June 2017 (The National, 22 June 2017; the report does not name the wadi or trail).

Terrain: constant climbing, many stone stairs (some without railings), narrow cliff-side ledges, loose rock and slippery ground (ECC Adventures, Pinay Hakawati, Wikiloc reviewers). Wear boots with good grip.
A Wikiloc author (undated) says part of the route crosses a dam construction area used by heavy trucks. Keep clear of vehicles and obey any signs or barriers.
The oasis can be reached from two starts, one low in Wadi Shah and one at the top of the mountain, and signs are changing. Know which route you are on and download an offline track.

Go with a companion, tell someone your route and return time (operator), and do not rely on mobile signal. Turn back if you are running late or the weather changes. Goats gather around walkers who take out food (Pinay Hakawati).
carry: At least 3 litres of water per person (operator); more in warm weather (a Wikiloc author says at least 4 litres)
Offline map or GPS track downloaded before you leave
Sturdy hiking boots with good grip
Fully charged phone and a power bank
Light layer for early starts in cooler months
Trekking poles (optional, for the steps and descent)
emergency: Police 999 (Ras Al Khaimah Police, as listed on visitjebeljais.com/jais-hiking); ambulance 998 and civil defence 997 (Ajman government emergency numbers page, ajman.ae; the numbers apply across the UAE). Police non-emergency line 901 (Gulf Today, 22 February 2024). Last checked October 2026.
driveNote: The operator's FAQ says Jebel Jais is about 2 hours by car from Dubai and about 45 minutes from Ras Al Khaimah city (visitjebeljais.com/faqs, last checked October 2026). The base camp is lower on the mountain road than the viewing deck. No source opened gave a drive time from Abu Dhabi.
intro: The names Sal Shehhah and Wadi Khammed are both used for this place in some sources: September 2026 press uses Wadi Khammed, and walkers and tour operators use Sal Shuha or Sal Shahha. That both mean the Hidden Oasis up Wadi Shah is probable, not confirmed. The Hidden Oasis is a green patch of palms and terraces reached from the Bear Grylls camp on the Jebel Jais road. The operator's guided walk to it is 7km, takes 3.5 to 4 hours and is graded beginner to intermediate. Trail works are under way and reports on whether it is open disagree, so check before you go.

_doubts: IDENTITY OF THE NAMES: 'Sal Shehhah' and 'Wadi Khammed' were merged into this one page because two researchers each found they most likely mean the Hidden Oasis up Wadi Shah. This is probable, not confirmed. Wadi Khammed appears only in September 2026 press about Marjan Lifestyle's Jebel Jais trail plans: 'Wadi Khammed to Hidden Oasis' or 'Wadi Khammed - Hidden Oasis' (The National, Khaleej Times, Gulf News, 15 September), 'Wadi Khammed (the Hidden Oasis)' (WhatsOn, 23 September), 'also known as the Hidden Oasis' at the bottom of Jebel Jais (Emirates 24|7, 19 September) and 'also called Hidden Oasis' (IndexBox, 27 September). None gives a map, start point or length. Sal Shuha or Sal Shahha is the local name for the oasis in ECC Adventures ('locally known as Sal Shuha'), Alpine Trekkers ('Sal Shahha'), a Wikiloc track ('Sal Shuha (Hidden Oasis)') and Komoot ('Sall Al Shaheh Hiking Trails'). No operator or government source uses either name. A fact-checker should ask Visit Jebel Jais, RAKTDA or Marjan Lifestyle where each name comes from.

SPELLING: no source uses the exact spelling 'Sal Shehhah' and no Arabic spelling was found; Arabic searches for variants of سل شحة returned nothing relevant. Variants searched for Khammed: Khamad, Khamid, Khammad, Khamed, Khamd and Arabic forms (وادي خمد, خميد, خمّد), with no relevant result in English or Arabic. Wadi Shah itself is also written Wadi Shehah, Wadi Shahha, Wadi Sheha and Wadi Shiha.

KHAMED MAY BE A SEPARATE PLACE: the Wikiloc seven-villages track names Shahha, Khamed and Musaibat as inhabited villages and calls Sal Shuha a ruin. That suggests Khamed could be a village or wadi near the oasis rather than a second name for it. The earlier draft text calling Wadi Shah 'Wadi Khamed' had no source of its own and is not repeated. If the Instagram author meant Khamed, this page may cover only part of what was meant.

NOT WADI SAL: Wikipedia's 'Wadi Sal' (25.781, 56.0646) is a different place, a farming wadi and the Habus village of Sal joining Wadi Bih, about 15km south-south-west. 'Sal' alone could mean either; 'Shehhah' points to Wadi Shah. If the Instagram author meant Wadi Sal, this page is for the wrong place.

WHICH WALK: the Hidden Oasis is a place, not an operator-named route. Sources describe an oasis-and-back walk (5 to 8.7km), the 9.6km Hidden Oasis Loop, the 11.6km Wadi Shah loop with the oasis at the midpoint (own guide on this site, slug wadi-shah), the 16km seven-villages loop and a point-to-point to Jebel Jais. This page covers only the walk to the oasis from the camp. It is also not confirmed that the operator's 'Hidden Oasis' on the Wadi Shah loop and on its guided Hidden Oasis Walk are the same oasis.

TWO STARTS: one start is low at the old Via Ferrata and Bear Grylls camp in Wadi Shah (operator guided walks, ECC Adventures, Wikiloc, Nukta). Another is near the last viewing deck at the top of the mountain, going down stone steps (Pinay Hakawati, published 2022, modified March 2026; 9 to 10km return, 689m, 'easy to moderate'). That blog also calls the oasis 'Hidden Oasis (Wadi of Giants)' and says a Wadi of the Giants trail branches from it; Visit Ras Al Khaimah's Wadi of the Giants blog (December 2022) mentions a hidden oasis at the end of that trail. Whether these are the same oasis, and which one the press calls Wadi Khammed, is unconfirmed. The page follows the camp start because it is the best documented and the one the operator guides. No coordinate was found for the top start.

OFFICIAL: set true because the operator publishes graded Hidden Oasis walks with lengths and times (Hidden Oasis Walk 7km, Loop 9.6km, Hidden Pond 9km) and says the Hidden Oasis trails need no guide. Against that: the operator lists the public Hidden Oasis trail itself with no length, grade or time, publishes no map or GPX, and uses neither Sal Shuha nor Wadi Khammed. The two input files disagreed (true and false). If 'official' should mean a published waymarked route with a map, this should be false.

GRADE IS EDITORIAL: Moderate. Sources: operator 'beginner to intermediate' (guided walk) and 'intermediate' (events list); ECC Adventures Intermediate+, 7 out of 10; Nukta 'Moderate' in its header but 'intermediate to advanced' in its text; Pinay Hakawati 'easy to moderate' (top start); Wikiloc comments 'Moderate+', with reviewers saying Difficult for the longer loop; Gulf News (29 October 2025) lists a Wadi Shah to oasis to Jais route among expert trails. Difficult ratings are for longer versions, not the oasis walk.

DISTANCE AND TIME CONFLICT: operator Hidden Oasis Walk 7.0km, 3.5 to 4 hours (shape not stated); operator February to April 2026 listing 8.5km, about 4 hours; Nukta 5km in 2 to 3 hours or a 15km loop in 6 to 8 hours; Pinay Hakawati 9 to 10km return, 3 to 5 hours; ECC Adventures 8.7km listed as one way, 3.5 to 4.5 hours; Gulf News 6.9km, 3 to 3.5 hours (to Jebel Jais, beyond the oasis); Alpine Trekkers 'about 7km round trip' for its connector with figures that do not match each other. The operator figure is used. These are different routes and versions.

CLIMB NOT CONFIRMED: climbM is null. The operator gives no climb for the Hidden Oasis Walk. ECC Adventures gives 900m (its own 'guide only' figure for 8.7km), a Wikiloc author 'more than 900m', Gulf News 942m (to Jebel Jais) and Pinay Hakawati 689m (top start). The 900m figures appear to include the climb on towards Shahha village and the Jebel Jais road. Komoot puts its Hidden Oasis point at 700m and walkers put the trailhead near 450m, which would suggest roughly 250m to the oasis, but that is my inference from two sources and is not used. Wikiloc and AllTrails pages returned 403, so no GPX or ascent was checked directly; Wikiloc was read through the loc.wiki mirror.

SHAPE: not stated by the operator for the Hidden Oasis Walk. ECC calls its hike one way, Pinay Hakawati describes a return on the same path, and Wikiloc describes loops with Wadi Shah. Left as not confirmed.

STATUS AND WORKS: the operator hiking page (read 6 and 8 October 2026) says the trails are open to the public and that works begin first at the Hidden Oasis; its home page still carries June and July pause posts; WOW-RAK (14 September 2026) says the whole mountain is closed with no reopening date; Khaleej Times (15 September) lists 'temporary signage ahead of season opening', which suggests the season had not yet opened; The National does not mention a closure. No dated reopening announcement was found. The works are on this exact place, so the route may be changing or restricted when you read this. Whether the works close the oasis path to walkers is not stated by any source. Re-check on the day of printing.

TRAIL STATE: dam works, RAKTDA, the Highlander trail and the 2026 rehabilitation (wider paths, easier grades, reinforced rock crossings, new signposts) mean older blogs describing boulder routes (hikerpatrick, hike done in 2021) and the undated Wikiloc warning about dam trucks may be out of date or may be current. Mapped tracks may not match the ground. ECC says RAKTDA has added railings.

TRAILHEAD: no operator coordinate. 25.90007, 56.14183 is the centre of four walker sources within about 100m: hikerpatrick.com (25.900073, 56.141830, published 16 April 2025), two Wikiloc tracks via loc.wiki (25.899797, 56.141828 and 25.900125, 56.141759) and Nukta's parking pin (25.8993105, 56.1420245, published 5 July 2024, modified 14 September 2024). The Road Reel gives 25.899871, 56.139836 for the Wadi Shah loop start, about 200m west. None was checked on a map. P-08 and the dam-works road limit in the Wikiloc warning were not verified against any official source.

PARKING, FEES, VEHICLE: no operator statement about the trail car park, capacity or charge. 'Free to walk' is the operator's wording for the trails, not for parking. The operator FAQ says the Jebel Jais road is paved and a normal car is enough, which I applied to the camp start. Pinay Hakawati says the top-of-mountain parking fills at weekends and holidays.

WHO RUNS IT: the walker-facing operator is Visit Jebel Jais (RAK Leisure; info@rakleisure.com). September 2026 press attributes the trail programme to Marjan Lifestyle, a subsidiary of Marjan (Khaleej Times); Emirates 24|7 says the RAK Tourism Authority announced the plans; IndexBox does not mention RAKTDA. Who is formally responsible for the Hidden Oasis trail is not confirmed.

RESCUES: none of the reports names the Hidden Oasis, Sal Shuha or Wadi Khammed; the Wadi Shah or Shahha area is used as context because the camp start is in Wadi Shah. Reports: 8 April 2021 nine people (Emarat Al Youm, Arabic); 22 February 2024 seven lost hikers in 'Wadi Shehah' (Gulf Today and Dubai Eye; Dubai Eye says the man who collapsed was airlifted, Gulf Today says he was carried out on a stretcher with the helicopter helping find a landing spot); 15 July 2026 an Emirati man stranded at about 2,000ft in Wadi Shah or Wadi Sheha (Gulf News, Khaleej Times, Al Khaleej; one report says severe exhaustion, another says trapped). A March 2021 Emarat Al Youm headline (12 March 2021) was seen but not opened and is not used. No deaths at Wadi Shah or the Hidden Oasis were found. The 2017 British hiker death on Jebel Jais (The National, 22 June 2017, 45 degrees Celsius that day) names no wadi and is used only for the heat point. A European hiker's death in RAK mountains (Gulf News, February 2023) names no location and is not used.

FLASH FLOODS AND FINES: no authority gives a Hidden Oasis or Wadi Shah flood rule or threshold. The flood advice rests on a Wikiloc author (washouts after rain, 2024), ECC and Pinay Hakawati (slippery after rain), Gulf News (18 December 2025, police warning to keep out of valleys) and The National (23 December 2025, standing water and shifting rocks). Wadi Shah recorded 247.4mm of rain in six days in April 2019 (Gulf News, 16 April 2019; the URL says 2474mm but the text says 247.4mm and the text is used). The Dh2,000 fine, 23 black points and 60-day impoundment in the Gulf News report are for entering a valley while water is flowing; I found nothing that says it applies to walkers, so it is not on the page. 'Do not start in or after rain' is my advice, not a quoted rule.

VILLAGES: the Wikiloc seven-villages author calls Sal Shuha a ruin and says Shahha, Khamed and Musaibat are inhabited; Wikipedia calls the settlement of Shah abandoned. Pinay Hakawati mentions an old village on the top approach, and ECC mentions villages of Baighit and Musaib near the Musandam border; those names rest on one source each and are not used. Do not expect help from residents.
RESTRICTIONS: no source mentions private land, a military area, fines or a permit specific to this route. Not finding one is not proof there is none. The dam works area may have its own restrictions.

RAKTDA WORDING: the operator says group size should be limited to 10 unless registered; Visit Ras Al Khaimah says groups over 10 'are obliged to inform' the authority by email with route, participants and timing. The 'licensed operators only' line comes from a Visit Ras Al Khaimah blog about the Wadi of the Giants hike (December 2022), not from a rule about this trail. Visit Jebel Jais says no guide is needed on public trails. All are reported. No registration form was found.

PRICES: operator guided-walk prices are 'from' prices on its hiking page; the February to April 2026 listing at AED 200 may be stale. ECC Adventures dates run 1 November 2026 to 2 January 2027 (AED 200 to 250 adult, AED 150 to 200 child, Dubai transport extra) and ECC says it can change or cancel dates.

NOT USED: Alpine Trekkers' claim of 400+ palms in 2008 to 2009 and a fire during road works, and ECC's 'Julfar' and Shehhi tribe wording (single-source promotional statements); Komoot's user tip calling its 874m 'Sall Al Shaheh' segment a 'very easy and simple short hike' (one review of a short segment); the 2018 Adventure Faktory summit trek.
SEASON: month scores are editorial, from the operator's October to April hiking season; the oasis is greenest in winter and after rain (ECC, Nukta).

SIGNAL AND SHADE: no operator source. Airial says signal can be spotty in the Jebel Jais mountains; ECC says coverage is better than before. Pinay Hakawati says the upper slope is in full sun with trees at the oasis.

PHOTO: no free photograph of the Hidden Oasis itself was found on Commons. Both input files used the same Commons file, Ciorraga's 'Another view of the Wadi Shah gorge.jpg' (CC BY-SA 4.0, 5 January 2023, camera location 25.892403, 56.123814 from EXIF, near the old Shah settlement, about 1.8km west of the trailhead). I did not see the image. The Wadi Shah page uses a different file of the same gorge. ShareAlike: credit and keep the licence. The Commons API was rate-limited, so only the files in Category:Wadi Shah were checked.
NO ABU DHABI DRIVE TIME found; omitted.

page.status: Part-official: Visit Jebel Jais lists graded guided Hidden Oasis walks and says the trails are open, but it publishes no map or waymarked route, trail works and new signs are under way, and whether the trail is open is not confirmed, so go with a licensed guide if you have not walked it before.
page.gradeBasis: Visit Jebel Jais, run by RAK Leisure, grades its guided Hidden Oasis Walk beginner to intermediate for people with moderate fitness. It publishes no grade for the public trail. Other sources range from easy to moderate to intermediate plus. Moderate is our reading of these sources.
route: This page covers the walk up Wadi Shah to the Hidden Oasis, not the whole Wadi Shah loop. The full loop passes the oasis at its midpoint and has its own guide at /trail/hikes/wadi-shah/.

You start at the Wadi Shah trailhead beside the Bear Grylls Explorers Camp, at about 450m above sea level, and walk up the wadi. Older accounts describe boulder-hopping with no path. Later accounts describe a built trail with stairs and zigzags past a dam, and a steady climb with stone steps and ledge paths. The operator says the first section is a steep climb.

The oasis is a patch of palms and farming terraces, greenest in winter and after rain. Most sources do not say whether the walk is a loop or an out-and-back. A second approach starts near the last viewing deck at the top of the mountain and goes down a long flight of steps, so the climb comes on the way back.
Waymarking is being changed. The operator is rebuilding trails and fitting new signs at the oasis from October, so the path and markers may differ from older maps.
page.distance: Visit Jebel Jais gives 7km for its guided Hidden Oasis Walk. Other sources give 5km to 10km, depending on start and version.
page.climb: Not confirmed. The operator gives no figure. Sources that give about 900m appear to include the climb beyond the oasis; others give 689m to 942m.
page.time: Visit Jebel Jais gives 3.5 to 4 hours. Other sources give 2 to 5 hours.
page.start: Wadi Shah trailhead next to the Bear Grylls Explorers Camp on the Jebel Jais road. The operator gives no exact point.
page.coordNote: The pin comes from four walkers' sources that agree within about 100m. None is an official coordinate. Confirm on site.
page.parking: Not confirmed. Walkers report parking next to the camp. The operator describes no car park. Check with Visit Jebel Jais.
page.vehicle: A normal car is enough on the paved Jebel Jais road, says the operator. Parking at the trailhead is not confirmed.
page.getting: Visit Jebel Jais says about 2 hours by car from Dubai, 45 minutes from Ras Al Khaimah city.
page.bestMonths: October to April, says Visit Jebel Jais. The oasis is greenest in winter. Do not walk it in summer.
page.startTime: Start early. The operator's guided walks leave at 8am. Finish well before dark.
page.shade: Little. Trees at the oasis give some shade; the slopes are in full sun.
page.water: None reliable on the route. Carry at least 3 litres each, as the operator advises.
page.signal: Not confirmed. Assume none and download an offline map.
page.fees: Visit Jebel Jais says the trails are free to walk on your own. No parking charge was found. Guided walks start at AED 200. Last checked October 2026.
page.permits: The operator says you do not need a guide, and no permit is listed. Groups over 10 must inform RAKTDA, the tourism authority, in advance. Last checked October 2026.
page.hours: No trail hours are published. The operator's FAQ says the mountain is open around the clock, which conflicts with the seasonal pause reported. Last checked October 2026.
page.closure: Not confirmed. The operator says the trails are open to the public. A local guide site (WOW-RAK, 14 September 2026) says the mountain is closed, with no reopening date, and the operator's home page still shows a summer pause. Trail works are under way at the Hidden Oasis itself (operator; The National, 15 September 2026), so sections may be closed or busy. Ask Visit Jebel Jais (info@rakleisure.com) or the camp (+971 56 501 5831). Last checked October 2026.
safety: Check the mountain and trail are open before you drive up. Reports disagree, and trail works are under way at the Hidden Oasis.
Do not start in or after rain. This is a wadi route, sections wash out, and wadis can flood when no rain is visible nearby. Wadi Shah recorded 247.4mm of rain in six days in April 2019.
Do not walk in summer. The operator advises October to April and says to avoid midday hiking in warm months.
Police have rescued hikers in the Wadi Shah area, including a lost group of seven in February 2024 and an Emirati man stranded at about 2,000 feet in July 2026. No report names the Hidden Oasis.
Expect a long climb, steep stairs, loose rock and narrow ledges. Wear boots with good grip.
Part of the area is a dam construction site, says one walker. Keep clear of trucks and obey any barriers or signs.
Know which start you are using. The oasis can be reached from the camp or from the top of the mountain, and signs are changing. Download an offline track.
Carry at least 3 litres of water each. Go with a companion, tell someone your route and return time, and do not rely on signal. Turn back if you are running late.
carry: At least 3 litres of water each
notConfirmed: The name. Sal Shehhah and Wadi Khammed are both used for this place in some sources, but that they mean the Hidden Oasis is probable, not confirmed. Wadi Khammed appears in September 2026 press (The National, Khaleej Times, Gulf News, Emirates 24|7, WhatsOn, IndexBox), none of which gives a map. Walkers and tour operators (ECC Adventures, Alpine Trekkers, Wikiloc) use Sal Shuha or Sal Shahha; no source uses the exact spelling Sal Shehhah.
Whether Khammed is a separate place. One Wikiloc track lists Khamed as an inhabited village distinct from the oasis.
Which walk is meant. The Hidden Oasis is a place, not a published route name. This page assumes the walk from the camp to the oasis. A second approach starts at the top of the mountain.
Whether the trail is open. Reports disagree, and works are under way at the oasis.
The climb, and whether the walk is a loop or an out-and-back.
The exact trailhead and parking. The operator says only near Jebel Jais Base Camp.
Waymarking. New signs are being fitted this season, so markers may change.

areaFull: Wadi Shah on the lower Jebel Jais mountain road above Ras Al Khaimah city. The walk starts near Jebel Jais Base Camp (Bear Grylls Explorers Camp) and climbs up the wadi to the Hidden Oasis. Other names in use: Sal Shuha or Sal Shahha (walkers and tour operators) and Wadi Khammed (September 2026 press). Whether all of these mean the same place is probable, not confirmed. Wadi Shah is also written Wadi Shehah. A second, different approach to an oasis of the same name starts near the last viewing deck at the top of the mountain.
